name: cake

attributes.attribute: is a symbolic object at feasts
is also called bannock or struan
is displayed to all in attendance at some sites
is won by the best dancer or athlete
is suggested by the blackened-piece custom

sources: Carmichael, Alexander. Carmina Gadelica: Hymns and Incantations. Hudson, N.Y.: Lindisfarne Press, 1992, 88, 624.
Anne Ross, "Lindow Man and the Celtic Tradition," in The Lindow Man: The Body in the Bog, ed. I. M. Stead, J. B. Bourke, and Don Brothwell (Ithaca, N.Y.: Cornell University Press, 1986), 162-169.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: At specific feasts, cake, sometimes called bannock, served as festive food and as part of a ritual. Some sites displayed the cake to everyone present. A champion dancer or athlete then won it. The winner took charge of breaking and distributing the cake. In some cases a portion of the cake was blackened. Whoever drew the dark share was named devoted. The custom may hint at an old rite of sacrificing a person.

okr.objective: Cake is a ritual symbol at Celtic feasts.
key_results: At certain feasts, cake, also called bannock, served as a ritual object.
The best dancer or athlete won the cake and distributed it.
One piece was sometimes blackened, and its drawer was called devoted.
The custom may suggest an ancient rite of human sacrifice.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
